title: How to Check and Remove Apps Connected to Google, Facebook and Instagram
html:
Every time you tap "Continue with Google" or "Log in with Facebook", that app gets a connection to your account, and it stays there until you remove it. Over a few years most people collect dozens of these. To clean up, open the connected-apps page on each platform, remove anything you do not recognise or no longer use, and then change the password on any account you are unsure about. It takes about 10 minutes, and it shrinks the number of companies that can reach your accounts.

Last updated: 29 Oct 2026. Menu names change between app versions and countries. I followed Google's and Meta's own help pages, and I flag below where a path may look different on your phone.

Why old connections are worth removing

When you log in to a new app with Google, Facebook or Instagram, you are not only skipping a password. You are also giving that app some access to your account, such as your name, email and profile picture, and sometimes more. Three things make old connections a real risk:

  • You forget them. An app you tried once in 2022 can still be connected today.
  • Small apps get breached or sold. You trusted the company at the time, but you did not choose whoever owns it now.
  • Some connections ask for more than a login. Reading your friends list, posting for you or reaching your calendar goes well beyond "sign in".

Removing a connection you do not use costs nothing. If you ever want the app again, you can sign in and allow it again.

Before you remove anything: do not lock yourself out

This is the step most guides skip. If you created an account in an app only with "Continue with Google", that app may have no separate password. If you remove Google's connection first, you can lose the easy way back in.

  • For apps you still use, open the app and check that you can log in with an email and password, or set one up first.
  • If the app is important, for example a bank, a work tool or something with paid content, leave it for last and look at its login options before you remove the link.
  • Keep a password manager or a written list of the logins you are changing. If you do not have one, see password managers for Android.

Step 1: Google (Sign in with Google and linked apps)

Google keeps these connections in one place. Open myaccount.google.com/linkedapps in your browser while signed in. Google's help page says the page groups apps by how they are connected:

  • Sign in with Google: apps where you used your Google account to log in.
  • Linked account: services that give Google access to your account on that service, for features such as a music app linked to Google.
  • Access to your Google Account: apps that can reach some of your Google data, for example Calendar. You can filter by Google product or by other account access.

To remove a Sign in with Google connection:

  1. On the linked apps page, choose Sign in with Google, then pick the app.
  2. Select See details.
  3. Select Stop using Sign in with Google, then Confirm.

To remove an app that has access to your Google data: choose Access to your Google Account, pick the app, select See details, read what it can access, then choose Remove access and confirm.

According to Google, removing Sign in with Google stops automatic sign-in to that app, but it does not delete your data inside the app. Removing a linked account means Google loses access to your account on that service, so features that depend on the link stop working on devices where you are signed in.

While you are in your Google account, run through the Google account security checklist too. The connected-apps page is only one of its settings.

Step 2: Facebook (Apps and websites)

On a computer, click your profile picture at the top right, then Settings & privacy, then Settings, and open Apps and websites from the left menu. Facebook's help pages describe removing an app by clicking Remove next to its name, with an option to tell the app that the login was removed, and then confirming. Facebook has moved settings around several times, so if you do not see it, search for "Apps and websites" in the Settings search box.

Facebook sorts apps into three groups, and the difference matters:

  • Active: you used the app in the last 90 days, so it can still reach the information you shared with it.
  • Expired: after 90 days of not using it, the app loses access to your non-public information, though it may still keep data it saved earlier. Using it again can make it active again.
  • Removed: you removed it, or the developer made it unavailable. It can reach only your public information.

Business integrations, which are apps with permission to manage Pages, groups, ads or messages, do not expire after 90 days. If you ever gave an app access to a Page you manage, check that part with extra care.

Also note what Facebook itself says: removing an app stops it accessing your non-public information through Facebook, but it does not necessarily delete the data the app already saved. If you turn off the platform integration entirely, you cannot log in to apps, games and websites with Facebook, so set up other logins first.

Step 3: Instagram (Apps and Websites)

Instagram's Help Center describes the web path as the menu, then Settings, then Website permissions under "Your app and media", then Apps and Websites. Open the Active tab and click Remove next to the app. On the phone app the same screen has been reported under Settings and then Security, and Meta has also been moving these controls into Accounts Center. I could not confirm one path that works on every version, so use the Settings search box and look for "Apps and Websites".

The same rule applies as on Facebook. A removed app keeps access only to public information, and it may still hold what it stored while you used it. Uninstalling the app from your phone does not remove its connection to your account. You have to remove the connection here.

How to decide what to remove

Do not try to judge every app by its name. Ask the same four questions for each one:

QuestionIf the answer is...Do this
Do I recognise this app?NoRemove it first, then check the account for anything odd.
Have I used it in the last 6 months?NoRemove it. You can reconnect later if you need it.
Does it need this much access?A quiz or photo app asking for friends, posting or messagesRemove it. A simple tool should not need that.
Is it my only way to log in there?YesAdd an email and password in that app first, then remove the link.

If you find an app you do not recognise

  1. Remove the connection straight away.
  2. Change the password of the account it was connected to, and of any other account that shares that password.
  3. Check the account's recent logins and turn on two-factor authentication. This guide explains which two-factor method to use.
  4. Look at your email for sign-in alerts you did not expect, and check whether your email appears in a leak with this data breach check.
  5. If the app posted, messaged people or changed settings without you, follow what to do when an account is hacked or locked.

Connections are also how some scams work. A message that asks you to "verify" your account by allowing an app is often a trick to get access without your password. How to spot a phishing email or message shows what to look for.

Ask the app to delete what it kept

Removing access ends the connection. It does not erase what the app already has. If you want the data gone, look in the app's own settings or privacy policy for an account deletion or data request option, or write to its support address and ask them to delete your account and data. Keep the reply. Our guide to privacy settings on Instagram, Facebook and WhatsApp covers the rest of what you control on those platforms.

Make it a habit

  • Before you tap "Continue with Google" on a new app, read what it asks for. If it wants more than your name and email, think again.
  • Repeat this check twice a year. It is quick the second time, because you only need to look at new entries.
  • Use a separate email address for apps you are only trying out.

What to do next

  1. Make sure you can log in to your important apps without the connection you are about to remove.
  2. Open myaccount.google.com/linkedapps and remove unused Sign in with Google connections.
  3. Open Facebook, then Apps and websites, and remove old active and expired apps.
  4. Open Instagram, then Apps and Websites, and remove what you do not use.
  5. Change the password of anything you could not explain, and turn on two-factor authentication.

Sources
